ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
Why the response to a single impulse describes the whole system
Stage 1: Describing signals
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
Before studying systems, you need a language for signals: a few basic shapes and two operations on the time axis, shifting and stretching.
Stage 2: A first system, the RC circuit
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
With the RC low-pass (Fig. 2) we can work out how a system responds to two typical inputs: a complex exponential and a step.
Stage 3: What an LTI system is
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
The RC circuit has two properties on which everything else rests: it is linear and time-invariant.
Stage 4: The convolution integral
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
With linearity and time invariance, the response to any signal can be computed from the response to a single short pulse.
Stage 5: Evaluating the convolution
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
The integral (4.2) has to be evaluated for concrete signals. The key is to draw both factors against the integration variable τ.
Stage 6: Rules of convolution
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
In many respects convolution behaves like multiplication. Each rule has a meaning for systems.
Stage 7: The Dirac impulse
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
The Dirac impulse is the limiting object from Stage 4. It is not an ordinary function.
Stage 8: Integrating and differentiating
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
The integrator and the differentiator are LTI systems. They link the step response to the impulse response, and they let you obtain the impulse response of the RC circuit from its step response.
Stage 9: Causal and stable
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
Two properties that every real system should have can be read directly from h(t).
Stage 10: Convolution without any system
ET3 · Chapter 1: LTI Systems and Convolution
Why the response to a single impulse describes the whole system

Overview: The Laplace Transform
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Every signal as a superposition of eᵖᵗ, and why an LTI system turns this into a multiplication
Stage 1: Why eᵖᵗ in particular
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
If you insert eᵖᵗ into the convolution integral, the result is H(p) eᵖᵗ: eᵖᵗ is an eigenfunction.
Stage 2: A signal made entirely of building blocks
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Stage 1 applies to a single building block. It becomes useful only if every signal can be built from building blocks eᵖᵗ.
The trick: damp, decompose, multiply back
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Every signal as a superposition of eᵖᵗ, and why an LTI system turns this into a multiplication
Region of convergence: which damping rates work
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Every signal as a superposition of eᵖᵗ, and why an LTI system turns this into a multiplication
Stage 3: Convolution becomes multiplication
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Stage 1 says what the system does to one building block. Stage 2 says that every signal consists of building blocks.
Stage 4: The integral becomes a sum
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
The conjecture taken literally: for the signals that system theory almost always deals with, the signal is a finite sum of complex exponentials.
Stage 5: Why the input is transformed too
ET3 · Chapter 2: Laplace Transform
Every signal as a superposition of eᵖᵗ, and why an LTI system turns this into a multiplication

Overview: Fourier Series and the Fourier Transform
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Every signal as a superposition of oscillations
Stage 1: Oscillations as eigenfunctions
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Of the building blocks eᵖᵗ, only the pure oscillations are used from now on. This stage shows what an LTI system does to them.
Stage 2: Periodic signals, the Fourier series
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
A periodic signal repeats itself after T. It can be built from oscillations, but only from very specific ones.
Stage 3: Power, convergence and LTI systems
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
How much does each harmonic contribute to the signal, how well does a truncated series approximate the signal, and what does an LTI system do with a periodic input?
Stage 4: From periodic to non-repeating signals
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
A single pulse is not periodic. But it can be regarded as a periodic signal with an infinitely long period.
Stage 5: Symmetries in the signal and in the spectrum
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Whether a signal is real, even or odd can be seen immediately from its spectrum. This stage derives the rules.
Stage 6: The rules of calculation (theorems)
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Instead of evaluating every integral anew, you use rules: what happens to the spectrum when the signal is shifted, compressed, differentiated or modulated?
Stage 7: Rectangle, si function and triangle
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Three transform pairs come up all the time. With the theorems, they follow from a single calculation.
Stage 8: Singular signals and line spectra
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
Constants, oscillations, the step and periodic signals are not absolutely integrable. With Dirac impulses in the spectrum they can still be transformed.
Stage 9: Hilbert transform and analytic signal
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
For a causal signal, the real and imaginary parts of the spectrum are linked: one determines the other.
Stage 10: Short-time Fourier transform
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
The spectrum S(f) describes a signal over all time. Speech or music, however, change their frequencies continually.
Stage 11: Fourier and Laplace, limits of existence
ET3 · Chapter 3: Fourier Series and Transform
When does the Fourier integral exist, and how is it related to the Laplace transform?
Key points

Overview: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
From the continuous signal to a sequence of numbers: sampling theorem, discrete convolution, DFT, FFT and z-transform
Stage 1: Signal classes and ideal sampling
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
What kinds of signals are there, and how is sampling described mathematically?
Stage 2: The spectrum of the sampled signal
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
What does sampling do to the spectrum? This stage shows that it repeats periodically.
Stage 3: The sampling theorem and reconstruction
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
When can the original be recovered exactly from the samples, and how?
Stage 4: Sampling in the frequency domain
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
The same principle holds with the roles swapped: if you sample the spectrum, the signal becomes periodic.
Stage 5: Discrete-time signals and discrete convolution
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
From now on, all calculations use only the sequences of numbers s(n). This stage carries convolution, elementary signals and LTI systems over to sequences.
Stage 6: A recursive system
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
The simplest IIR system shows how feedback produces an infinitely long impulse response and when the system is stable.
Stage 7: The discrete-time Fourier transform
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
What spectrum does a sequence of numbers have? It is the spectrum of the ideally sampled signal, computed directly from the samples.
Stage 8: The discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
Sₐ(f) is a continuous function, but a computer needs finitely many numbers. For a sequence of finite length, finitely many samples of the spectrum are enough.
Stage 9: FFT and fast convolution
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
The DFT needs M² multiplications. The FFT gets by with roughly M lb M.
Stage 10: Changing the sampling rate, decimation and interpolation
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
A sequence can afterwards be represented at a lower or higher rate. The same rules apply to the spectrum as for the original sampling.
Stage 11: The z-transform
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems
Just as the Laplace transform extends the Fourier transform (Chapter 2), the z-transform extends the discrete-time Fourier transform: first weight exponentially, then transform.
Key points
ET3 · Chapter 4: Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems

Overview: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
Distortionless transmission, ideal lowpass, complex envelope and group delay
Stage 1: The distortionless system
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
What exactly should a “good” transmission achieve? And with which characteristic quantities do you measure how far a system deviates from it?
Stage 2: The ideal lowpass
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
The ideal lowpass passes all frequencies up to f_g unchanged and blocks all frequencies above.
Stage 3: Step response and rise time
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
How does the ideal lowpass respond to a step? How fast does it rise, and how far does it overshoot?
Stage 4: Causal approximation
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
How do you build something that comes as close as possible to the ideal lowpass? You delay the impulse response and cut off the rest.
Stage 5: Echo method and pulse-shaping filters
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
How do you design a lowpass with less overshoot? You assemble the impulse response from shifted si functions and choose their weights.
Stage 6: Discrete-time lowpass filters, window design
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
How do you design a digital lowpass? Exactly like the causal analog one: take the ideal lowpass, delay it, truncate it with a window.
Stage 7: The ideal bandpass and its equivalent lowpass
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
A bandpass passes a band around the center frequency f₀. This stage shows that it can be described completely by a lowpass and the frequency f₀.
Stage 8: Complex envelope and quadrature components
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
What holds for systems also holds for signals: a bandpass signal is a lowpass signal on a carrier.
Stage 9: Bandpass signal through a bandpass system
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
What the envelopes are good for: how a bandpass acts on a bandpass signal can be calculated entirely in the lowpass domain.
Stage 10: Quadrature circuit and bandpass sampling
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
How are the quadrature components obtained in practice? And how many samples does a bandpass signal need?
Stage 11: Phase and group delay in a bandpass
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
Why are there two delays? Because the carrier and the envelope can be delayed differently.
Stage 12: Discrete-time bandpass and highpass filters
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
Digital bandpass and highpass filters are obtained from a lowpass by modulation.
Key points
ET3 · Chapter 5: Lowpass and Bandpass Systems
Distortionless transmission, ideal lowpass, complex envelope and group delay
Overview: Correlation Functions
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
How similar are two signals, and how is the energy distributed over frequency?
Stage 1: Energy and power
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
Before comparing signals, you need a measure of their “size”. In system theory this is the energy, or, for infinitely long signals, the power.
Stage 2: Measuring similarity, the correlation coefficient
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
How do you measure with a single number how similar two signals are? You measure how large their difference is.
Stage 3: Correlation function and correlation product
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
An echo is similar to the transmitted pulse, but shifted. You therefore compare for every shift τ.
Stage 4: Energy spectral density
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
What is the Fourier transform of a correlation function? It shows how the energy is distributed over the frequencies.
Stage 5: Correlation and LTI systems
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
What does an LTI system do to the ACF and the energy spectral density? And how do you measure a system with cross-correlation?
Stage 6: Correlation of bandpass signals
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
Correlation functions of bandpass signals, too, are computed with the complex envelopes (Chapter 5).
Stage 7: Discrete-time and periodic correlation
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
For samples, the integral becomes a sum. With the DFT, correlations can be computed quickly.
Key points
ET3 · Chapter 6: Correlation Functions
How similar are two signals, and how is the energy distributed over frequency?
Overview: Random Signals
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
Mean values, distributions, power spectral density, noise in systems and the optimal receiver
Stage 1: The random process
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
How do you describe a signal whose waveform you do not know? You imagine many signals of the same kind and average over them.
Stage 2: Stationarity and ergodicity
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
You never have an infinite ensemble, usually only a single signal. When is that enough?
Stage 3: Mean value, power, variance
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
The most important first-order averages and their intuitive meaning.
Stage 4: Autocorrelation, covariance and cross-correlation
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
How fast does a random signal change? The ACF tells you: how similar the signal still is to itself after the time τ.
Stage 5: Distribution function and probability density
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
Averages do not tell everything. How often does a signal take which values?
Stage 6: Joint distribution, independence, uncorrelatedness
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
Two random variables at once: when are they related, and what follows for their sum?
Stage 7: The Gaussian distribution
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
Why is noise so often Gaussian, and how do you calculate with the Gaussian distribution?
Stage 8: Random signals in LTI systems, power spectrum
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
What does an LTI system do to a random signal? Each sample function is convolved.
Stage 9: White noise and thermal noise
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
The most important model for disturbances: noise with the same power density at all frequencies.
Stage 10: The matched filter (correlation filter)
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
A known pulse s(t) arrives corrupted by noise. With which filter does it become most clearly visible at the sampling instant T?
Stage 11: Error probability in binary reception
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
The receiver has to decide: was the pulse sent or not? How often is it wrong?
Stage 12: Discrete-time random signals
ET3 · Chapter 7: Random Signals
Everything also holds for sequences of random numbers, with sums instead of integrals.
Key points

Overview: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
ET3 · Chapter 8: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
Two supplementary topics: signals as vectors, waves on electrical transmission lines
Stage 1: Signals as vectors, the orthogonal expansion
ET3 · Chapter 8: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
The Fourier series decomposes a signal into oscillations. The same works with any system of orthogonal functions.
Stage 2: The transmission-line equations
ET3 · Chapter 8: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
So far, lines were ideal connections. If a line is long compared with the wavelength, a signal needs a noticeable time to travel through it.
Stage 3: Waves under sinusoidal excitation
ET3 · Chapter 8: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
With phasors, the partial differential equations become an ordinary differential equation in position.
Stage 4: The lossless line
ET3 · Chapter 8: Orthogonal Expansion and Transmission Lines
Without losses (R'=G'=0), the characteristic impedance and the velocity become independent of frequency.
